newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican general denies troop pullout.
newsitem.headline: Mexican general denies troop pullout.

text.p: Mexico's military denied reports earlier on Monday that it was pulling troops out of the southeastern Chiapas state close to where Zapatista guerrillas are holed up.
Witnesses said earlier that the army was withdrawing troops from areas in the impoverished state where they have kept Zapatista rebels surrounded during on-off peace talks for nearly two years.

"It is not a case of a withdrawal of troops. It is a readjustment of our forces in order to keep them in better conditions and to maintain security in the state and fight narco-trafficking," Gen. Mario Renan Castillo, commander of the Seventh Military Region, told reporters.
He confirmed reports that some troops had been moved, but said the soldiers had only traveled about 30 kilometers (19 miles) for regrouping before being assigned to other camps.

Media reports speculated the movements might constitute a withdrawal aimed at bringing the rebels back to the negotiating table to find a permanent solution to the uprising they launched for democracy and indian rights in January 1994.
Rebel complaints of the extensive military presence were partly responsible for a break-off in talks late last year.

A Reuters reporter who witnessed the scene, as well as local residents, said three former military camps close to the town of San Andres Larrainzar -- site of the stalled peace negotiations -- were clearly vacated.
San Andres Larrainzar is some 15 miles (24 km) north of San Cristobal de las Casas, the colonial city where the rebels launched their uprising in a 10-day burst of fighting more than 3-1/2 years ago.
Last week Castillo announced that 5,000 soldiers in the areas of conflict would be relieved.

The troop movement occured about two weeks before President Ernesto Zedillo's state of the nation address on Sept. 1, and Mexican newspapers said it could be an olive branch extended to the Zapatistas.
The troops apparently moved out quietly in the middle of the night late last week.

"By the time we noticed, they had already burned their shacks and destroyed their trenches," Joaquin Gomez, a who lives near the former San Cayetano camp, told Reuters. "They took out all their tanks in the middle of the night."

A coalition of non-government peace groups known as Conpaz says the government has some 40,000 troops in 250 camps in 80 of the state's 111 municipalities. The soldiers greatly outnumber the Zapatistas.
